23. We have considered the submissions of the Petitioner. The trial run is an elaborate process defined in the Grid Code whereby the entity is required to furnish documents and test reports and to carry out real-time operation in coordination with the RLDC after giving due notice. The minimum capacity for a trial run is 50 MW, except for an entity under Regulation 4.1(e) of the GNA Regulations, which may conduct a trial run for the capacity of connectivity to enable such entity to achieve the trial run. An entity, while seeking connectivity, is fully aware that it must complete the trial run at full capacity together. 24. We note that the Petitioner delayed in commissioning the entire capacity. We do not find the instant case a fit case for us to exercise our power to relax to permit the Petitioner to conduct a trial run for a smaller capacity. Accordingly, the Petitioner's prayer to permit phase-wise commissioning of its 36 MW Wind Power Project is rejected.

Allowing PSPCL to go back on the promise made would be inequitable as it would put the Petitioners at a financial loss. The Hon’ble Supreme Court has held that if a party acts upon the promise made, that is sufficient to invoke the principle of promissory estoppel. In the instant case, as stated above, the Petitioners have acted upon the promises made by PSPCL in the PSA and therefore, the Petitioners are right in invoking the principle of promissory estoppel, and PSPCL is estopped from going back on the promises made in the PSA, and it has to adhere to its obligations under the PSA. 64. We have already discussed the misplaced reliance on the order of the APTEL dated 24.9.2024 in Appeal No. 167 of 2020. It is also necessary to highlight that the said decision does not deal with the well-settled maxim _nullus commodum capere potest de injuria sua propria_ (no man can take advantage of his own wrong), which is a fundamental principle of equity and justice, whereas it is conspicuously applicable here. The facts of the said decision did not require the invocation of this maxim, but the facts of the present case demand it. The Commission cannot mechanically apply the proposition of one case to the facts of another case, especially when the same would subvert equity and not uphold the law. Thus, we hold that the Order dated 24.9.2024 in Appeal No. 167 of 2020 is distinguishable on facts and does not compel a decision in favour of PSPCL.
